title: Why airlines sell more tickets than seats

beats.text: Airlines sell more tickets than there are seats. On purpose.
Why? Because a seat is perishable. Once the plane takes off, an empty seat earns nothing, ever.
And on every flight, some passengers simply don't show up. Missed connections, changed plans, traffic.
So airlines use years of data to predict no-shows, route by route, even day by day.
Then they sell a few extra tickets to cover the gap. Most of the time, the math works.
When it doesn't, they offer money to volunteers, and raise the offer until someone says yes. It's still cheaper than an empty seat.
That's the mechanism. Overbooking isn't a mistake. It's a bet on human unreliability.

title: Why the same airline seat has different prices

beats.text: Two passengers on the same flight can pay very different prices for the same seat.
That's because airlines don't set one price per flight. They split the cabin into fare buckets, around twenty of them, each with its own price and rules.
Each bucket holds a limited number of seats, and the cheapest bucket sells first.
When a cheap bucket sells out, the next one opens at a higher price.
What triggers it isn't who's shopping. It's how fast the flight is filling, plus demand forecasts and competitors' prices.
And it can go the other way. If a flight sells slowly, cheaper buckets can reopen.
That's the mechanism. The same seat, sold at the price of the moment.

title: Why movie popcorn costs so much

beats.text: A movie ticket isn't where the cinema makes its money.
Studios can take most of the ticket price. One industry veteran says as much as seventy percent.

data.title: Ticket price (illustrative split)
data.note: Up to ~70%, varies over a film's run

beats.text: But the cinema keeps every cent you spend at the snack counter.
By commonly cited estimates, snacks are about a fifth of a theater's revenue, yet around forty percent of its profit.
Meanwhile, one older estimate puts a theater's overall profit margin at just four percent.
So pricey popcorn isn't random. It's where the business earns its keep.
That's the mechanism. The ticket gets you in. The popcorn pays the bills.
Why does the medium popcorn cost almost as much as the large?
Say a cinema sells a small for three dollars and a large for seven.
Then it adds a medium at six fifty. Nobody is really meant to buy it.
But next to that medium, the large suddenly looks like a bargain.
Psychologists call it the decoy effect: a third option that's worse than one choice, and only partly worse than the other.
It's not magic, though. Research suggests it works under specific conditions, like when the options are close in value.
That's the mechanism. An option designed to be ignored, so another one gets picked.
Why does everything cost ninety-nine cents instead of a round number?
Two ninety-nine and three dollars are only one cent apart. Your brain doesn't see it that way.
Researchers call it the left-digit effect. The first digit changes, so the price feels like a different category.
A study by New York University researchers found the effect is stronger when the nine changes that first digit.
It also gets stronger when the price sits close to a comparison price, like a sale next to a regular price.
It doesn't work every time. But often enough that retailers keep using it.
That's the mechanism: a one-cent change that your brain treats as a bigger one.
Airlines didn't always charge you to check a bag.
In two thousand eight, many US airlines began charging for bags, then for reservation changes, priority boarding, and more.
Researchers describe it as a way to charge different customers different prices, born from revenue pressure in the two thousands.
By two thousand sixteen, US airlines collected about seven billion dollars a year from just bag and change fees, according to the Government Accountability Office.
The catch: the ticket price no longer shows the full cost. Consumer advocates say that makes airlines harder to compare.
That's the mechanism. Split the trip into pieces, and charge for the pieces.

title: Why Costco never raises its hot dog price

beats.text: Costco has charged one dollar fifty for its hot dog combo since nineteen eighty-five.
Not a cent more, for decades. And the company's chief financial officer has publicly said the price is safe.
It's widely described as a loss leader: a cheap item meant to pull people in. Costco hasn't said it loses money on it.
Employees have described it as a perk for members, and a pleasant last stop before checkout.
And in Costco's member magazine, an executive wrote that the price shows a company can earn a fair markup and still pay its bills.
Either way, a price that never changes becomes a signal. It tells you what kind of store this is.
That's the mechanism. A promise you can taste, for a dollar fifty.

title: Why free trials ask for your card

beats.text: Why does a free trial ask for your credit card?
In one older study, two percent of visitors started a trial that needed a card. Ten percent started one that didn't.

data.title: Visitors who start a trial (2012 study)

beats.text: But those who did start were far likelier to pay. A newer analysis of two hundred business software products found about thirty percent of card-required trials turned into paying customers, over five times the rate without a card.
The card works as a filter. It keeps casual browsers out, and leaves people already leaning toward buying.
There's a trade-off, though. One study found card-required trials had lower end-to-end conversion, because so few people got started.
That's the mechanism. Fewer people start, but the ones who do are far more likely to pay.
